messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 49

# Case Vignette: Raymond

Raymond is a 71-year-old married man who has worked as a security guard at a downtown shopping mall for the past eleven years. He is a broad-shouldered, quietly dignified man who chooses his words carefully and tends to sit with his back to the wall in any room he enters — a habit his wife, Carol, has learned not to comment on anymore.

Fourteen months ago, Raymond was on duty when a man entered the mall's main atrium and detonated an explosive device. Raymond was stationed near the food court, close enough to feel the concussive wave move through his chest before he fully understood what had happened. He remembers the sound — not as a bang, but as a silence that swallowed everything and then gave it back wrong. He remembers the smoke, and a woman's shoe lying by itself near the fountain, and the fact that he kept moving toward the blast rather than away from it, because that was his job. Three people died that afternoon. Raymond helped carry a teenage boy out of the debris who did not survive the night.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond returned to work because he did not know what else to do with himself. Standing in the rebuilt atrium in his uniform felt important — like proof that something had continued. But the proof felt hollow. He found himself scanning every face that walked through the entrance doors with an intensity that exhausted him by noon. He began writing down the clothing descriptions of men who entered alone, filling small notebooks he kept in his breast pocket. His supervisor noticed he had stopped taking breaks.

At home, Raymond is present in body but often somewhere else entirely. He sits through dinner with Carol and their son's family on Sunday afternoons and finds himself unable to follow the conversation, pulled back instead to the particular quality of light in the atrium that day, the way the dust hung in the air like something suspended in amber. He does not tell Carol about these moments. He has always been a man who managed things privately, and he sees no reason to change that now, though he recognizes, dimly, that the distance between them has grown.

He sleeps poorly. When he does sleep, he often wakes between two and four in the morning with his heart already hammering, the details of the dream dissolving before he can name them but leaving behind a residue of dread that takes hours to lift. He has begun sleeping on the couch so as not to disturb Carol, though she has told him more than once that she would rather be disturbed.

Raymond does not think of himself as someone who was traumatized. He thinks of himself as someone who did his job and is now having trouble with sleep. He is skeptical of the word *trauma* and uses it reluctantly, if at all. What he will say, if pressed, is that the mall does not feel like the same place it was before, and that he does not feel like the same person. He notices that he is quicker to anger than he used to be — a sharpness that surprises him and that he apologizes for afterward, quietly, without explanation.

What troubles Raymond most is not the nightmares or the vigilance or even the anger. It is a particular moment that returns to him unbidden, several times a day: the instant just before the explosion, when he looked directly at the man who carried the device and felt nothing unusual — no instinct, no warning, nothing. He had been standing right there. He had been doing his job. Raymond is 71 years old, and he has built his sense of himself around the belief that he is someone who pays attention. That belief no longer holds the way it once did, and he is not yet sure what to put in its place.
